CERTIFICATED TEACHER DISMISSAL FOR CAUSE AND THE MORRISON "FITNESS TO TEACH" STANDARD — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Example Unified School District

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — CERTIFICATED TEACHER DISMISSAL FOR CAUSE
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as Grade 5 Classroom Teacher with Example Unified School District. This information sheet describes the statutory scheme that governs the dismissal of a permanent certificated employee of a California K-12 school district for cause — California Education Code sections 44929.21 and 44932 through 44944, within Article 3 (Resignations, Dismissals, and Leaves of Absence) of Chapter 4 of the Education Code — together with Morrison v. State Board of Education (1969) 1 Cal.3d 214, the California Supreme Court decision that narrowed several of that statute's conduct-based dismissal grounds to require a showing that the conduct indicates the employee's unfitness to teach. It is separate from this project's State Civil Service Disciplinary Due Process and Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act documents, neither of which addresses this Education Code chapter, and from a private-sector at-will or wrongful-termination analysis, which does not apply to a permanent certificated public school employee dismissed under this statutory scheme. It is not a written answer, a request for a hearing before a Commission on Professional Competence, an administrative appeal, a writ of mandate petition, or a superior court filing, and completing it does not initiate, extend, or preserve any deadline under Education Code section 44934, section 44944, or any other statute or collective bargaining agreement. Completing it does not establish that Example Unified School District took, or failed to take, any specific action described in this sheet, or that any statement here is true.

PERMANENT (TENURED) STATUS: HOW IT IS ACQUIRED UNDER EDUCATION CODE SECTION 44929.21
This document addresses the dismissal of a "permanent employee" as that status is defined by the Education Code — not a probationary or temporary certificated employee, whose own, more limited procedural rights come from different Education Code provisions this document does not address. In a school district with an average daily attendance of 250 or more, an employee in a position requiring certification qualifications who is employed for two complete consecutive school years and reelected for a third becomes a permanent employee of the district at the start of that third year, and the governing board must notify the employee by March 15 of the second year if it does not intend to reelect the employee, or the employee is deemed reelected.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "(b) Every employee of a school district of any type or class having an average daily attendance of 250 or more who, after having been employed by the district for two complete consecutive school years in a position or positions requiring  certification qualifications, is reelected for the next succeeding school year to a position requiring certification qualifications shall, at the commencement of the succeeding school year be classified as and become a permanent employee of the district."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44929.21 (California Legislative Information text), two-year path to permanent (tenured) status for a certificated employee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44929.21.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the two-consecutive-year path to permanent status that applies to a probationary period commencing in the 1983-84 fiscal year or later (Education Code section 44929.21(b)); an earlier three-consecutive-year path in subdivision (a) applies only to a probationary period that commenced before that date and is not analyzed here. This document does not address a school district with an average daily attendance under 250 pupils, whose permanent-status and dismissal procedures differ in ways this document does not research; it does not address community college faculty, whose parallel tenure and dismissal provisions appear in a different part of the Education Code (beginning around section 87600) that this document does not cover; and it does not determine whether a specific employee has, in fact, satisfied this section's reelection and notice requirements. The raw fetched HTML also renders a non-breaking space (not a regular space) immediately after the subdivision letter, and a doubled space between "requiring" and "certification" in the same sentence — both confirmed identical in two independently fetched copies of this section using distinct User-Agent strings — and both are preserved exactly, rather than corrected, in the quoted citation below.

THE STATUTE'S OWN LIST OF CAUSES FOR DISMISSING A PERMANENT CERTIFICATED EMPLOYEE
Education Code section 44932(a) provides that a permanent certificated employee shall not be dismissed except for one or more of eleven causes the statute itself enumerates. They include immoral conduct (a category the statute further defines to include, but not be limited to, a narrower category the statute calls "egregious misconduct"), unprofessional conduct, advocating or committing acts of criminal syndicalism, dishonesty, unsatisfactory performance, evident unfitness for service, a disqualifying physical or mental condition, persistent violation of or refusal to obey school laws or reasonable board regulations, conviction of a felony or of a crime involving moral turpitude, violation of a specified statute or Government Code provision, and alcoholism or other drug abuse that makes the employee unfit to instruct or associate with children.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "(a) A permanent employee shall not be dismissed except for one or more of the following causes:"
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44932(a) (California Legislative Information text), introductory sentence limiting dismissal to enumerated causes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44932.)
  "(1) Immoral conduct, including, but not limited to, egregious misconduct."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44932(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), immoral conduct as a cause for dismissal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44932.)
  "(2) Unprofessional conduct."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44932(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), unprofessional conduct as a cause for dismissal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44932.)
  "(6) Evident unfitness for service."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44932(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text), evident unfitness for service as a cause for dismissal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44932.)
  "(9) Conviction of a felony or of any crime involving moral turpitude."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44932(a)(9) (California Legislative Information text), conviction of a felony or crime involving moral turpitude as a cause for dismissal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44932.)
  Known gap: This clause's citations quote the introductory sentence and four of the eleven lettered causes verbatim (immoral conduct, unprofessional conduct, evident unfitness for service, and conviction of a felony or crime involving moral turpitude); the remaining seven causes are described narratively above rather than quoted exactly. In the raw fetched HTML, leginfo renders a non-breaking space (not a regular space) immediately after each subdivision's numbering, for example "(1) Immoral conduct" — confirmed identical in two independently fetched copies of this section using distinct User-Agent strings — and that non-breaking space is preserved exactly, rather than corrected, in each quoted citation below. This clause does not determine whether any specific conduct falls within one of these eleven statutory causes, and does not address subdivision (b)'s separate suspension-without-pay procedure for unprofessional conduct.

MORRISON V. STATE BOARD OF EDUCATION: CONDUCT-BASED GROUNDS REQUIRE A NEXUS TO FITNESS TO TEACH
In Morrison v. State Board of Education, the California Supreme Court considered a state board's revocation of a teacher's life diplomas for "immoral and unprofessional conduct" and "acts involving moral turpitude" under a predecessor Education Code provision using language closely resembling several of section 44932's current causes. The court held that these general, conduct-based terms cannot be applied in the abstract; conduct falls within them only if it indicates that the individual is unfit to teach. California courts applying section 44932's own immoral-conduct, unprofessional-conduct, and moral-turpitude causes to a permanent certificated employee's dismissal have since drawn on this same fitness-to-teach nexus requirement, reasoning that the statutory language Morrison construed is substantially the same language section 44932 now uses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "In the instant case the terms denote immoral or unprofessional conduct or moral turpitude of the teacher which indicates unfitness to teach."
  — Morrison v. State Board of Education, 1 Cal.3d 214 (1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1159400/morrison-v-state-board-of-education/)
  Known gap: Morrison itself did not arise under Education Code section 44932 — it reviewed the State Board of Education's revocation of a teaching credential under a former Education Code section 13202, a different statute directed at credentialing rather than a governing board's dismissal of its own certificated employee, decided in 1969 and since renumbered and amended. This document has not independently researched and does not cite a specific California Court of Appeal decision expressly extending Morrison's nexus holding to a section 44932 dismissal proceeding, nor confirmed that every one of Morrison's specific holdings remains undisturbed by later statutory amendment (section 44932 was itself last amended in 2015, well after Morrison was decided, including the addition of the "egregious misconduct" sub-definition Morrison's 1969 opinion could not have addressed) or by later case law. A reader considering this nexus doctrine in connection with a section 44932 proceeding, rather than a credential-revocation proceeding, is relying on an analogy between two related but textually distinct statutes, not on a holding that construed section 44932 itself.

MORRISON'S NON-EXHAUSTIVE LIST OF FACTORS BEARING ON FITNESS TO TEACH
Morrison identified a set of factors a board may consider in determining whether particular conduct indicates unfitness to teach, including the likelihood that the conduct adversely affected students or fellow teachers, the degree of that anticipated adversity, and the proximity or remoteness in time of the conduct. The opinion's footnoted list continues with several additional considerations described only narratively here rather than quoted exactly: the type of teaching certificate held, any extenuating or aggravating circumstances surrounding the conduct, and the praiseworthiness or blameworthiness of the underlying motive. The opinion closes the list with the likelihood that the conduct will recur, and the extent to which disciplinary action might inflict an adverse impact or chilling effect on the constitutional rights of the teacher involved or of other teachers. The court framed all of these factors as relevant only to the extent they help determine whether the teacher's future classroom performance and overall impact on students are likely to meet the board's standards.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "In determining whether the teacher’s conduct thus indicates unfitness to teach the board may consider such matters as the likelihood that the conduct may have adversely affected students or fellow teachers, the degree of such adversity anticipated, the proximity or remoteness in time of the conduct,"
  — Morrison v. State Board of Education, 1 Cal.3d 214, 229 (1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1159400/morrison-v-state-board-of-education/)
  " the likelihood of the recurrence of the questioned conduct, and the extent to which disciplinary action may inflict an adverse impact or chilling effect upon the constitutional rights of the teacher involved or other teachers."
  — Morrison v. State Board of Education, 1 Cal.3d 214, 229-230 (1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1159400/morrison-v-state-board-of-education/)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two separate, non-adjacent spans of Morrison's factor list rather than the entire passage verbatim, because the source opinion interrupts the list with footnote markers between several of the factors (for example, immediately after "the proximity or remoteness in time of the conduct," and again after several of the factors that follow). The three factors in between — type of certificate held, extenuating or aggravating circumstances, and praiseworthiness or blameworthiness of motive — are described narratively above rather than quoted, to avoid presenting footnote-interrupted text as a single contiguous quotation. This clause does not indicate how a court or a Commission on Professional Competence would weigh these factors against each other in any specific case, and Morrison's own list is expressly non-exhaustive ("the board may consider such matters as"), meaning a decisionmaker is not limited to only these factors.

WRITTEN NOTICE AND STATEMENT OF CHARGES BEFORE DISMISSAL (EDUCATION CODE SECTION 44934)
Before dismissing a permanent employee for a cause specified in section 44932, the governing board must act on written charges — either filed by another person and duly signed and verified, or formulated by the board itself — and, by majority vote, give the employee notice of its intention to dismiss at the expiration of 30 days from the date the notice is served, unless the employee demands a hearing within that period. The statute requires that any written statement of charges be specific enough that the employee can prepare a defense: it must specify instances of behavior and the acts or omissions constituting the charge, state, where applicable, the statutes and rules the employee is alleged to have violated, and set forth the facts relevant to each charge.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "the governing board of the school district may, upon majority vote, except as provided in this article if it deems the action necessary, give notice to the permanent employee of its intention to dismiss or suspend him or her at the expiration of 30 days from the date of service of the notice, unless the employee demands a hearing as provided in this article."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44934(b) (California Legislative Information text), written charges and 30-day dismissal notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44934.)
  "Any written statement of charges shall specify instances of behavior and the acts or omissions constituting the charge so that the employee will be able to prepare his or her defense."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44934(c) (California Legislative Information text), specificity requirement for a written statement of charges (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44934.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the general notice-and-charges procedure in section 44934; it does not address section 44934.1, a separate procedure the statute specifies applies instead when a dismissal or suspension is based solely on egregious-misconduct charges, nor the rule in section 44934(d) permitting charges to be amended less than 90 days before a hearing only on a showing of good cause. It does not address whether a specific school district's charges in a specific case meet this specificity requirement, and does not address the separate procedures many school districts follow instead under a collective bargaining agreement adopted pursuant to Government Code section 3543.2(b), which section 44934(b) itself states can displace the suspension procedure this section otherwise authorizes.

THE RIGHT TO A HEARING BEFORE A COMMISSION ON PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE
An employee who demands a hearing after receiving notice under section 44934 is entitled to a hearing conducted under the Administrative Procedure Act's formal hearing chapter. Unless both parties waive it in writing and stipulate to a single administrative law judge instead, that hearing is conducted by a three-member Commission on Professional Competence: one member selected by the employee, one selected by the governing board, and one who is an administrative law judge of the Office of Administrative Hearings, who serves as chairperson, is a voting member, and is responsible for assuring that the legal rights of the parties are protected at the hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "one member of the commission shall be selected by the employee, one member shall be selected by the governing board of the school district, and one member shall be an administrative law judge of the Office of Administrative Hearings who shall be chairperson and a voting member of the commission and shall be responsible for assuring that the legal rights of the parties are protected at the hearing."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44944(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), composition of the Commission on Professional Competence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44944.)
  Known gap: This clause does not address the detailed hearing-timeline rules in section 44944(b) — including the six-month deadline to commence a hearing and seven-month deadline to close the record after a demand for hearing, the extraordinary-circumstances and good-cause continuance exceptions to those deadlines, or a separate rule limiting evidence of conduct occurring more than four years before the notice was filed — nor the eligibility and selection-timing rules for commission members, nor the compensation rules for a commission member who is a current or retired school district employee. It does not address whether a specific district has adopted a collective bargaining agreement that displaces the suspension authority referenced elsewhere in this statutory scheme.

THE COMMISSION'S DECISION, ITS THREE POSSIBLE DISPOSITIONS, AND ITS BINDING EFFECT
The Commission on Professional Competence decides by majority vote and must prepare a written decision containing findings of fact and determinations of issues, resolving into exactly one of three dispositions: that the employee should be dismissed, that the employee should be suspended for a specific period without pay, or that the employee should not be dismissed or suspended. The statute states that the commission's decision is deemed to be the final decision of the governing board of the school district itself — the board does not separately vote to adopt or reject it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The decision of the Commission on Professional Competence shall be made by a majority vote, and the commission shall prepare a written decision containing findings of fact, determinations of issues, and a disposition that shall be, solely, one of the following:"
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44944(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), majority-vote decision and its three possible dispositions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44944.)
  "The decision of the Commission on Professional Competence shall be deemed to be the final decision of the governing board of the school district."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 44944(d)(4) (California Legislative Information text), the decision is deemed the governing board's final decision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=44944.)
  Known gap: This clause does not address section 44944(d)(2)'s limitation on a not-dismissed-or-suspended decision resting on nonsubstantive procedural errors (only a prejudicial procedural error may support that disposition), nor section 44944(d)(3)'s separate limitation on the commission's power to dispose of a dismissal charge by imposing probation or another alternative sanction instead. It does not address how a governing board or an employee may seek judicial review of the commission's decision — that avenue exists under a separate body of administrative-mandate law (Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5 and related case law) that this document has not researched. It also does not address the suspension-without-pay disposition's own separate statutory limits, which apply only where suspension proceedings were properly authorized under section 44932(b) or section 44933 in the first place.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — CERTIFICATED TEACHER DISMISSAL INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 8, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

It does not itself determine that Example Unified School District did, or did not, comply with any provision of this statutory scheme with respect to Jordan Lee, is not a written answer, hearing demand, administrative appeal, writ of mandate petition, or court filing, is not filed with any agency or court by completing it, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statutes, the employing district's own board policies or applicable collective bargaining agreement, or a licensed attorney.]

citations.quote: one member of the commission shall be selected by the employee, one member shall be selected by the governing board of the school district, and one member shall be an administrative law judge of the Office of Administrative Hearings who shall be chairperson and a voting member of the commission and shall be responsible for assuring that the legal rights of the parties are protected at the hearing.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not address the detailed hearing-timeline rules in section 44944(b) — including the six-month deadline to commence a hearing and seven-month deadline to close the record after a demand for hearing, the extraordinary-circumstances and good-cause continuance exceptions to those deadlines, or a separate rule limiting evidence of conduct occurring more than four years before the notice was filed — nor the eligibility and selection-timing rules for commission members, nor the compensation rules for a commission member who is a current or retired school district employee. It does not address whether a specific district has adopted a collective bargaining agreement that displaces the suspension authority referenced elsewhere in this statutory scheme.

expectedJSON.body: The Commission on Professional Competence decides by majority vote and must prepare a written decision containing findings of fact and determinations of issues, resolving into exactly one of three dispositions: that the employee should be dismissed, that the employee should be suspended for a specific period without pay, or that the employee should not be dismissed or suspended. The statute states that the commission's decision is deemed to be the final decision of the governing board of the school district itself — the board does not separately vote to adopt or reject it.

citations.quote: The decision of the Commission on Professional Competence shall be made by a majority vote, and the commission shall prepare a written decision containing findings of fact, determinations of issues, and a disposition that shall be, solely, one of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44944(d)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the decision is deemed the governing board's final decision
citations.quote: The decision of the Commission on Professional Competence shall be deemed to be the final decision of the governing board of the school district.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not address section 44944(d)(2)'s limitation on a not-dismissed-or-suspended decision resting on nonsubstantive procedural errors (only a prejudicial procedural error may support that disposition), nor section 44944(d)(3)'s separate limitation on the commission's power to dispose of a dismissal charge by imposing probation or another alternative sanction instead. It does not address how a governing board or an employee may seek judicial review of the commission's decision — that avenue exists under a separate body of administrative-mandate law (Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5 and related case law) that this document has not researched. It also does not address the suspension-without-pay disposition's own separate statutory limits, which apply only where suspension proceedings were properly authorized under section 44932(b) or section 44933 in the first place.
